blocks.text: Another opinion bases the distinction here on the difference between insects that one is otherwise accustomed to catch for the sake of their usefulness and those that one leaves uncaught. Rashi counts among the former the locusts and the גוין, which, as mentioned, he likewise explains as a kind of locust, and among the latter the hornet and the gnats; the more correct division, however, is probably that only the locusts belong to the former insects, since they were eaten and were even the object of a regular trade (§. 384), while to the latter belong wasps, hornets and gnats, since the two former kinds of insects are left undisturbed by people on account of their painful sting alone.
On the reading גוי for זבי, by which the Tosephot (on Nidda 17a s.v. מקרקש) wish to denote the wasps, cf. §. 285.
The Hornet.
צירעה (Tanit 13a), pl. צירעין (Sabbat 106b); further: זיבורא, fem. זיבוריתא (A. Sara 17b), pl. זבורי (Sanhedrin 109b), and ערעיתא (Sabbat 80b).
For the woman's name דבורה the Talmud writes זיבורתא (Megilla 14b, and on this §. 109).

[p. 304] The hornet, expressly described as a winged insect (Pesachim 24b), is, as is well known, very dangerous on account of its sting when it is provoked*), and is therefore frequently mentioned alongside the scorpion (Kerithoth 3b and often). Its sting would infallibly kill a nine-year-old child unless one ground moss that grows around a palm tree in water and gave it to the child to eat (Ketuboth 50a). The Tosephoth, however, regard this not as a cure but as a preventive, and the former probably rightly, for, as is claimed, 4 hornets can kill even a horse. Once, too, a hornet killed a man by a sting on the forehead (Sabbath 80b). It is said here that the insect came out of the wall; indeed, hornets usually inhabit hollow trees, but sometimes also buildings (Voigt l. c. 4. p. 288). If someone has swallowed a hornet, he must drink very sharp (אינגרא, aigre) vinegar if he still wishes to gain time to draw up a will (A, Sara 12b). As the most inhuman cruelty of the inhabitants of Sodom it is recorded that they once smeared with honey a girl who had handed bread to a poor man, and then exposed the unfortunate creature to the stings of the hornet (Sanhedrin 109b). Prayers were therefore ordained for the extermination of this insect (Tanit 14a). Crushed flies laid on the wound are said to be a remedy against its sting (Sabbat 77b), further the urine of a child 40 days old (ibid. 109b). Above all, the person stung must guard against catching cold (A. Sara 28b).
On the stone bumblebee cf. below §. 512.
The Ninevite Hornet.

The Ninevite hornet (צירעה שבנינוה) is so dangerous that it may be killed even when unprovoked, and indeed on the Sabbath (Sabbat 121b). Ordinarily the hornet is peaceable and simply must not be provoked (Voigt l. c. 4. p. 288); accordingly, that Talmudic hornet must be much more dangerous. According to Jalkut Schimoni (Exod. fol 98, col 1) the hornet kills by poison; as is well known, however, every bee has a poison vesicle at the base of its sting (Voigt loc. cit. p. 269).

In our Talmud passage צירעה שבנינוה and זבוב שבארץ מצרים (Egyptian fly, §. 427) stand side by side, and both insects are probably meant in Jes. 7, 18; there that fly is called זבוב אשר בקצה יארי מצרים "fly at the banks of the Nile of Egypt," and our hornet דבורה אשר בארץ אשור "bee in the land of Assyria"; Nineveh was, as is well known, the capital of that empire.
The Fig Gall Wasp.

The fig gall wasp, also called the fig borer (Cynips psenes), which lays its eggs in the fruits of the wild fig, is called פה דתאנה "opening of the fig" (Sabbat 90a), because the wasp lays the eggs into the small opening at the top of the fig. It is dangerous to swallow, and someone who ate the fig together with the hatched worm died as a result (ibid.). Cf. §. 440.

I take the liberty of adding to this article that in considering our wasp we must admire the divine omnipotence with reverence and adoration. Our insect is the means of carrying the male pollen into the female flower of the fig. The fig flower has a very small opening, so that the entry of the male pollen by the wind is made very difficult; the winged insects emerging from the pupae of our wasp now carry that dust on their wings into the female flower.
The Beetle.
The חפושית, and whatever resembles it, belongs to the unclean insects (Chulin 67b); by that addition is understood the numerous genus of beetles, of which a fair number are mentioned in the Talmud.
Rashi explains that word by אישקרבוטי, Escarbot.

If it lies in water, the water enters through the mouth and passes out through the anus, since the interior of the beetle is shaped like a simple tube and allows that passage (Para 9, 2). Thus Aristotle says (Naturg. 4, 7, 7): Inwardly, the mouth is directly joined by the intestine, which in most insects runs straight and simple to the outlet and is coiled only in a few. Zeller (Tractatus de [p. 306] Vacca rufa, Amsterd. 1711) erroneously translates חפושין in the relevant passage in Maimuni (ch. 9, §. 11) by piscis (fish), in doing which he no doubt had חיפושא (§. 345) in mind.
The Aramaic name חפושית corresponds to the Arabic خُنْفَسآء [khunfasāʾ]*).
The Cockchafer.
Against earache the fat**) of the large חיפושתא is recommended (A. Sara 28b). The insect is called: גמלניתא חיפושתא.
Rashi explains the word חיפושתא: אשקרבוט ובלשון כנען קרוקים, i.e. Escarbot, in another language***): "Kerukim."
